newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German tandem still pedals towards EMU.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German tandem still pedals towards EMU.

text.p: Like tandem cyclists who sometimes hit a bumpy stretch, the Franco-German couple appears to be holding together and heading for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Economists say that agreements on EMU reached at a European Union summit in Amsterdam this week show the Paris-Bonn axis is still working despite very different philosophies on economics.

"There is a great amount of understanding on both sides for the political gestures that are required to appease a sceptical public," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "What emerges to me is really two countries operating in tandem."
She noted that the franc-mark link, the linchpin of a single currency, has held intact throughout the EMU tumoil after the French left's upset election victory on June 1.

Compared with the currency crisis of four years ago when the French franc plunged to 3.55 per mark from 3.36 in just six weeks, this month it has barely moved between a low of 3.3860 and high of 3.3680.
In Amsterdam, France's new Socialist-led government backed down on a call to review a "stability pact" which limits budget deficits of countries particpating in EMU.
This was seen by Bonn as a key to selling the euro to a German public nervous about giving up the stable mark.

In return, French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin won a pact to boost growth and jobs -- allowing him to tell his domestic audience he had kept his election promise to put unemployment at the top of the European agenda.

In the end, the dispute finished the same way as all previous battles, as a balance of France's need for an interventionist economic policy and Germany's insistence on leaving key decisions on monetary policy to an independent central bank.

"The Franco-German couple has never been a pre-established harmony. It has been, is, and will be tomorrow a system to create convergence from positions that can be spontaneously different," French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine told Europe 1 radio on Wednesday.
That said, Paris and Bonn still face power struggles ahead on the road to EMU.
"For the markets it's not going to be a straight line. We are going to have a lot of volatility," Owens-Thomsen said.

Vedrine acknowledged that it was getting harder to keep the Franco-German duo in step given domestic demands on both governments. "It's less automatic to find convergence...it's a bit more laborious," he said.
Two big fights lie ahead, budgetary and monetary.
Until recently Bonn had the upper hand on both but political and economic problems in Germany are likely to force it to give ground on the budgetary front.

"The German position has weakened in Europe. The old ideas of Keynesianism are becoming more popular and Germany has no longer the power to reject this," said Eckhard Schulte, economist at IBJ in Frankfurt.

British economist John Maynard Keynes advocated public spending to ensure full employment, an idea popular in the 1960s but which fell out of fashion in the 1980s as many governments made free-market reforms.
Schulte said that even in Germany there were increasing calls for more active management of economic demand, in parallel with the new French government's desire to end austerity in Europe.

In practice, that may mean Germany has to accept the looser interpretation of the Maastricht treaty demanded by Jospin. He has said he will not impose new austerity just to cut the public deficit to precisely three percent of gross domestic product -- a key target laid down in the treaty for would-be EMU members.
That in turn could open the door to Italy joining EMU at the start -- favoured by France and resisted by Germany -- even if its deficit/GDP ratio overshot.

But on the monetary front, France may have to tone down its demands for political co-ordination of exchange rates and for a euro which is not overvalued. Instead it may have to accept a balance of power which tips towards the independent European Central Bank.

It has already dropped the label "economic government", which French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said did not go down well with France's partners, in favour of a call for an "economic pillar" in Europe.

Germany insisted on making the independence of the central bank virtually untouchable in the Maastricht treaty. For Bonn, the principle of non-interference by politicians in the exchange rate is virtually sancrosanct.
